from typing import Tuple

    print(x_flattened[:, channel].clone().mean()) 
```
I get the correct results ...

I also uninstalled the torch package in google collab, and installed it again from pip with the same results ...

One thing I see is that for NumPy it gets the same wrong results when the array is float32,
The same array, when moved to Cuda & cupy, gets the correct results for the complete array mean.

If I reduce the number of rows of the array, then it works fine in numpy and pytorch
`x_flattened = x_flattened[:5000000]`

The ATen code does just `array.sum()._div(n)` and this seems to lead to heavy precision issues in this case just for the sum operator. But even if we delete this code and use the `MeanOps` as in the GPU, the results won't change. However, for cuda this works fine. 🤔

This is easily reproducible in NumPy and torch by doing:
```
import numpy
a=numpy.random.rand(51200000, 3)
print(a.mean(axis=0))
a=a.astype(numpy.float32)
print(a.mean(axis=0))
```

However, the result in google collab is puzzling as I would expect it to happen in the local environment too.

Should we allow to do type promotion for partial results of the reduction?
The `combine` function might use inputs and return data different than the `reduction` function, but this will require several changes in the core reduction routines.

---

[peterbell10]: The problem is that it calculates a running sum
```
sum = 0
for x in xs:
	sum += x
```

When `sum` is large enough, `x` is just a rounding error by comparison and so `sum += x` doesn't increase the `sum`. CUDA does a similar sum, but only for partial sums which are calculated in parallel before being added together. So, instead of `big + small = big` it's doing `medium + small = medium`, followed by `medium + medium = big`. The same is true for local machine vs colab. My local machine has more CPU cores, so `binary_kernel_reduce_vec` splits the sum into more intermediate partial sums.

Note that `double` should have the exact same precision issues, it will systematically under-report the sum and mean of large tensors. It will just only effect the lower mantissa bits.

One way to fix this would be to avoid calculating the sum and instead use the [`iterative mean`](http://www.heikohoffmann.de/htmlthesis/node134.html). This keeps the accumulator on the same order of magnitude as the data, so the addition doesn't lose precision. Unfortunately, it is also much slower because it does many more divisions and also it can't be vectorized in the current `Reduce.h` machinery.

I think it makes sense to instead focus on the accuracy of the `sum`. @emcastillo's suggestion of using a `double` for the accumulator should help here. However, that would also have performance implications as well as leaving the `double` precision sum inaccurate. 

I think a better option would be to split the reduction into more partial sums, similar to how it's done on GPU. That should have minimal performance implications and will also fix `double` tensors in exactly the same way.

Thoughts?

---

[gchanan]: removing 1.5.1 milestone based on @peterbell10's comments; at a minimum, it's not a trivial fix.

---

[emcastillo]: Exactly, I explored the idea of modifying the cpu reduction algorithm to do partial reductions instead of just the running sum. But I wasn't sure of the implications for other routines.
I can keep working in this direction if you think it is reasonable @peterbell10.

---

[ezyang]: cc @ngimel

---

[peterbell10]: I don't think it makes sense to modify the generic reduction algorithm. Most other users of `binary_kernel_reduce_vec` don't really have this problem: `and`, `or`, `min`, `max`.

`prod` would depend on the input; if all elements are magnitude > 1 then it definitely doesn't help. For some mixtures of > 1 and < 1 then it could prevent `inf`s popping up.

---

[ngimel]: This is a similar issue https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/37234 where the difference in results is attributable to contiguous vs discontiguous tensors (one is using vectorized kernel, another does not) and different number of cores on the machines. 
I agree that making `sum` accumulate in double has performance implications. `cumsum` for floats accumulates in double on cpu, and `cumsum` on floats is slower than cumsum on doubles.

---

[emcastillo]: I think that cuda splitting the sums in multiple partial sums comes naturally from how the reduction algorithm is implemented. In the CPU should we try to do the reduction manually for the sum without using the binary_kernel_reduce_vec template as `cumsum` does?

Also, how should we decide the grain in which we split the partial sums? I guess that a number similar to the block size of the gpu should suffice.

---

[emcastillo]: I have been tracing the execution of the sum reduction and what I found just confirms all said above.

First, if instead of doing 
```python
a = numpy.random.rand(51200000, 3)
a = torch.tensor(a, dtype=torch.float32)
b = a.sum(axis=0)
print(b)
```
I do 
```python
a = numpy.random.rand(3, 51200000)
a = torch.tensor(a, dtype=torch.float32)
b = a.sum(axis=1)
print(b)
```
Then the result is more or less correct (float32 rounding errors still happening but now is expected).
The difference here is that the reduction is now contiguous and before it was outer in `binary_kernel_reduce_vec`, so this issue seems to be the same that @ngimel pointed out.

When doing a contiguous reduction with a large row, the row is split with the number of threads so we have several partial sums, but when we are doing an outer reduction, then a thread calculates an entire column, so this problem appears just as @peterbell10 said.

---

[emcastillo]: Just pushed a PR that batches the reductions for cpu
#39512

---

[peterbell10]: It seems we've doubled up a bit here. See #39516 for an alternate solution that doesn't require a batch size and has good error performance for any length of tensor.

comments:
[ShawnZhong]: I don’t have multiple GPUs on hand to verify this, but my guess is to call https://pytorch.org/docs/master/cuda.html#torch.cuda.manual_seed_all first to set the same random seed across all GPUs.

---

[ssnl]: @ShawnZhong this is a deterministic operation, so random seed shouldn't matter.

edit: should -> shouldn't

---

[sdaulton]: shouldn't*

---

[thoglu]: the first device agrees with cpu right? Why does the second printed tesnor not contain a "cuda:0", it looks just like the first cpu tensor. Since icdf calls erfinv, and erfinv does some newton steps, maybe different precision somehow creeps in? although that should only happen for values right at the boundary of [0,1], not all of the random values, so that is really weird.

---

[ngimel]: There's something wrong with how we are setting device guard. Easy repro without distributions:
```
import torch

x = torch.rand(10, dtype=torch.double, device="cuda:1")
val = torch.tensor(1.)
y=x * val
torch.cuda.synchronize()
print("ok")
y=val * x
torch.cuda.synchronize()
print("ok") #not ok, illegal memory access
```

---

[ngimel]: @sdaulton if you need a quick workaround, you can do 
```
import torch
x = torch.rand(10, dtype=torch.double, device="cuda:1")
normal = torch.distributions.Normal(0,1)
with torch.cuda.device_of(x):
    normal.icdf(x)
```

---

[kurtamohler]: I found some more details about this issue, but I don't yet know what the solution is. The functions in `build/aten/src/ATen/CUDAType.cpp` create an OptionalDeviceGuard to match the device of `self`. For instance:
```
 Tensor mul_Tensor(const Tensor & self, const Tensor & other) { 
     const OptionalDeviceGuard device_guard(device_of(self));
     return at::native::mul(self, other);
 }
```

In @ngimel's repro above, for the `val * x` case, `self` will be the scalar `val`. Scalar tensors have the device type `cpu`, so the OptionalDeviceGuard will be for cpu, not cuda. This problem doesn't cause an issue (seemingly accidentally?) in the usual case where `x.device()` is `cuda:0`, because PyTorch makes `cudaGetDevice()` default to index 0. But for the same reason, the `cuda:1` case breaks because the OptionalDeviceGuard does not know that we should be switching over to `cuda:1`, so when the `mul` operation is executed, we end up trying to access a `cuda:1` buffer from `cuda:0`. As @ngimel showed, we can work around the issue by explicitly telling pytorch to use `cuda:1`. But if we tried to do something like `torch.tensor(1.) * torch.tensor(..., device="cuda:0")` inside of the `with torch.cuda.device_of(x)` in her code snippet, it would break for the same reason.

Here are some examples that might help explain what I mean:

This `cuda:1` operation **fails** because `x` doesn't match `torch.cuda.set_device()` setting:
```
torch.cuda.set_device(0)
x = torch.rand(10, dtype=torch.double, device="cuda:1")
val = torch.tensor(1.)
y = val * x
torch.cuda.synchronize()
```

This `cuda:0` operation **fails** because `x` doesn't match `torch.cuda.set_device()` setting:
```
torch.cuda.set_device(1)
x = torch.rand(10, dtype=torch.double, device="cuda:0")
val = torch.tensor(1.)
y = val * x
torch.cuda.synchronize()
```

This `cuda:0` operation **works** because `x` does match `torch.cuda.set_device()` setting:
```
torch.cuda.set_device(0)
x = torch.rand(10, dtype=torch.double, device="cuda:0")
val = torch.tensor(1.)
y = val * x
torch.cuda.synchronize()
```

This `cuda:1` operation **works** because `x` does match `torch.cuda.set_device()` setting:
```
torch.cuda.set_device(1)
x = torch.rand(10, dtype=torch.double, device="cuda:1")
val = torch.tensor(1.)
y = val * x
torch.cuda.synchronize()
```

It seems like we need something either before or inside of `mul_Tensor()` (and all other functions in `CUDAType.cpp`) that recognizes when `self` is a scalar, and then create a DeviceGuard from `other` instead. I'm not sure how that should be done in a generalized way that applies to all the operations. I might need some help with thinking of a solution.

---

[ngimel]: Since this situation only occurs when gpu_kernel_with_scalars is used, a general solution that changes the codegen to decide where to put device guard seems like an overkill, and probably we can put an additional deviceGuard here https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/d627f2b174136b720dcc99380e2b98f535d1f169/aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/Loops.cuh#L79-L107.

---

[kurtamohler]: Thanks @ngimel ! I made a patch.

## To Reproduce

```python

title: PyTorch issue 41865
body:
## 🐛 Bug

I am experimenting with dynamic quantization as described here:
https://pytorch.org/blog/introduction-to-quantization-on-pytorch/

I got a pretty good speedup when running with a single thread. (This is a GRPC server application that serves pytorch models). However, I do not see any improvement when using multiple threads and processing multiple concurrent requests. This does not happen when dynamic quantization is not being used: I see pretty good scaling up to about 10 threads. The CPU utilization when running with 10 threads but without quantization is well over 700%. However, when dynamic quantization is enabled, CPU load peaks around 150%, meaning that most of the cores sit idle.

This leads me to believe that python's GIL is the culprit. I noticed that in many parts of the code, pytorch does the following:

pybind11::gil_scoped_release no_gil;

But this does not happen in qlinear_dynamic.cpp which runs on dynamic quantization. This again implies that when dynamic quantization is used, GIL does not get released. This would certainly explain why we see improved performance with one thread but not with multiple threads.

## To Reproduce

Steps to reproduce the behavior:

1. Set OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 environment variable.

If you call `torch.hub.load_state_dict_from_url()` on a file saved in the new zipfile serialization format, it raises `RuntimeError('Only one file(not dir) is allowed in the zipfile')`.

## To Reproduce

Steps to reproduce the behavior:

1. Upload a state dictionary file saved using the vanilla `torch.save()` to a server.
1. Call `torch.hub.load_state_dict_from_url()` to that url.
1. You'll see the `RuntimeError` raised.

We discovered this as part of the effort to support pytorch 1.6 with pytorch lightning. Here's one of the failed test runs: https://github.com/PyTorchLightning/pytorch-lightning/runs/920684391

body:
## 🐛 Bug

Since updating to version 1.6, when trying to access `model.state_dict()` of a older pytorch trained models (where model is a subclass of torch.nn.module), I'm getting a `ModuleAttributeError`.

## To Reproduce

Steps to reproduce the behavior:

```
torch.load("path/to/model", map_location='cpu')
print(model.state_dict())
```
where the model was trained with an older version of pytorch.

The output is
```
  File "/home/oliviermt/miniconda3/envs/projections/lib/python3.7/site-packages/torch/nn/modules/module.py", line 900, in state_dict
    module.state_dict(destination, prefix + name + '.', keep_vars=keep_vars)
  File "/home/oliviermt/miniconda3/envs/projections/lib/python3.7/site-packages/torch/nn/modules/module.py", line 900, in state_dict
    module.state_dict(destination, prefix + name + '.', keep_vars=keep_vars)
  File "/home/oliviermt/miniconda3/envs/projections/lib/python3.7/site-packages/torch/nn/modules/module.py", line 897, in state_dict
    self._save_to_state_dict(destination, prefix, keep_vars)
  File "/home/oliviermt/miniconda3/envs/projections/lib/python3.7/site-packages/torch/nn/modules/module.py", line 860, in _save_to_state_dict
    if buf is not None and name not in self._non_persistent_buffers_set:
  File "/home/oliviermt/miniconda3/envs/projections/lib/python3.7/site-packages/torch/nn/modules/module.py", line 772, in __getattr__
    type(self).__name__, name))
torch.nn.modules.module.ModuleAttributeError: 'GaussianSmearing' object has no attribute '_non_persistent_buffers_set'
```

I was able to make it work by adding the following lines after the the `torch.load`:
```
for mod in model.modules():
     if not hasattr(mod, "_non_persistent_buffers_set"):
            mod._non_persistent_buffers_set = set()
```
If it's expected behaviour, then ignore this issue, but I would guess it's not.
Thanks a lot!

## Expected behavior

Not needing to add those 3 lines.

title: PyTorch issue 42265
body:
## 🐛 Bug
We observed a big increase in inference latency after adding `torch.inverse()` in the code path. After investigation and comparison with moving the op to CPU we found that there is a huge difference in performance of that op on GPU vs CPU.
The matrix size in our case is 4x4 which small for the GPU but `torch.inverse()` should be using `magma` library which has heuristics to move the op to CPU. We didn't see any magma invocations as well.

Based on @ptrblck suggestion we tried `inverse` on batched matrix to see if that made any difference but that also didn't result in any improvement.

**Performance Difference:**
```
╰─ python torch_inverse_exp.py
GPU Time: 8.78560 ms
CPU Time: 0.07149 ms
cpu/gpu: 122.90x
```
We increased the matrix dimensions to 1024x1024 but even then GPU is slower than CPU:
```
╰─ python torch_inverse_exp.py
GPU Time: 17.25289 ms
CPU Time: 9.54982 ms
cpu/gpu: 1.81x
```
## To Reproduce
Here is the snippet of code which can be run to reproduce the performance difference:
```
import torch
import time

a = torch.randn(4,4).cuda()
torch.cuda.synchronize()

num_iter = 100
def test1():
    s = time.time()
    for i in range(num_iter):
        x = torch.inverse(a)
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    e = time.time()
    gpu_time = ((e - s)/num_iter)
    return  gpu_time

def test2():
    s = time.time()
    for i in range(num_iter):
        b = a.to('cpu')
        d = torch.inverse(b)
        y = d.to('cuda')
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    e = time.time()
    cpu_time = ((e - s)/num_iter)
    return  cpu_time

gpu_time = test1()
print("GPU Time: {:.5f} ms".format(gpu_time*1000))

cpu_time = test2()
print("CPU Time: {:.5f} ms".format( cpu_time*1000))

print("cpu/gpu: {:.2f}x ".format(gpu_time/cpu_time))
```
**Run:** `python <script_name>`

title: PyTorch issue 42305
body:
## 🐛 Bug

The following trick for mypy

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/269ec767cabe9c47baab18e58fad5d6485d4e65d/torch/nn/modules/module.py#L223-L239

introduced with 1.6 leads to pylint warnings

```
W0223: Method '_forward_unimplemented' is abstract in class 'Module' but is not overridden (abstract-method)
```

when extending `nn.Module` for custom modules.

## To Reproduce

Steps to reproduce the behavior:

1. Create MWE
```python
from torch import nn

class MyModule(nn.Module):
    def forward(self, x):
        return x
```
2. run pylint
```console
$ pylint --disable=all --enable=abstract-method mwe.py
mwe.py:4:0: W0223: Method '_forward_unimplemented' is abstract in class 'Module' but is not overridden (abstract-method)

```

## Expected behavior

No warnings if `forward` is implemented.

## Environment

```

Is debug build: No

OS: Ubuntu 20.04.1 LTS

[conda] Could not collect
```

## Additional context

* I am using pytorch in project with many custom modules where the CI runs pylint. Since upgrading to torch 1.6 I therefore get a large number of warning. Since pylint is quite widespread, I suppose this problem may occur for other users as well.
* I am unsure whether the "bug" type of issue is correct. However, it seemed to be the best fit.

cc @ezyang @malfet @rgommers
comments:
[VitalyFedyunin]: CC @ezyang

---

[ezyang]: Ugh, this sucks. @mberr, I don't have a lint easily setup right now, but if we "hide" the `raise NotImplemented` in some way (e.g., by putting it in a lambda and then immediately invoking it) does that appease the lint? If so I'd be happy to take the patch.

---

[mberr]: > Ugh, this sucks. @mberr, I don't have a lint easily setup right now, but if we "hide" the `raise NotImplemented` in some way (e.g., by putting it in a lambda and then immediately invoking it) does that appease the lint? If so I'd be happy to take the patch.

Replacing https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/269ec767cabe9c47baab18e58fad5d6485d4e65d/torch/nn/modules/module.py#L223-L227 by

```python
    # Trick mypy into not applying contravariance rules to inputs by defining
    # forward as a value, rather than a function.  See also
    # https://github.com/python/mypy/issues/8795
    def _forward_unimplemented(self, *input: Any) -> None:
        def f(*x):
            raise NotImplementedError
        return f(*input)
```

stops pylint from raising the `abstract-method` in the MWE from above. However, now it also fails to correctly detect cases where `forward` is not overridden, e.g.

```python
from torch import nn


class MyModule(nn.Module):
    def forward(self, x):
        return x


class MyModule2(nn.Module):
    pass
```

does not raise any `abstract-method` warning.

---

[mberr]: @ezyang I think I found a solution, cf. #42356

---

[mberr]: @ezyang It seems like the fix lead to a failure for one specific build, `pytorch_macos_10_13_py3_test`, but I cannot make much sense out of the error log I see there.

title: PyTorch issue 43414
body:
## 🐛 Bug

A simple division operation: `g = x/y` could produce numerical instability if multiple backward is applied.
This is because the derivative is calculated by `-grad * self / (other * other)` (see `tools/autograd/derivatives.yaml` in `div.Tensor`).
The `other` tensor is squared in one backward operation, so multiple operation will raise `other` to the power of `2^n` and can reach `inf` or `0` very quickly.
A simple fix should be sufficient: by replacing the derivative calculation to `-grad * result / other`, but it makes a bunch of tests fail (I'm not sure why).

## To see the problem

    import torch

    class Div2(torch.autograd.Function):
        @staticmethod
        def forward(ctx, x, y):
            z = x / y
            ctx.save_for_backward(x, y, z)
            return z

        @staticmethod
        def backward(ctx, gz):
            x, y, z = ctx.saved_tensors
            gx = Div2.apply(gz, y)
            gy = Div2.apply(-gz*z, y)
            return gx, gy

    def example(g, y, n):
        gs = [g.item()]
        for i in range(n):
            g, = torch.autograd.grad(g, (y,), create_graph=True)
            gs.append(g.item())
        return gs

    if __name__ == "__main__":
        a = 1e-8
        x = torch.tensor(a, requires_grad=True)
        y = torch.tensor(a, requires_grad=True)
        n = 4
        factorial = lambda i: 1 if i < 2 else i * factorial(i-1)
        print("Div1 (current implementation):")
        print(example(x / y, y, n))
        print("Div2 (proposed implementation):")
        print(example(Div2.apply(x, y), y, n))
        print("Actual:")
        actual = [(-1)**i*factorial(i)/(a**i) for i in range(n+1)] # [1.0, -1/a, 2/(a*a), -3*2/(a*a*a), 4*3*2/(a**4)]
        print(actual)

Output: 

    Div1 (current implementation):
    [1.0, -100000000.0, 1.99999983976448e+16, -inf, nan]
    Div2 (proposed implementation):
    [1.0, -100000000.0, 2.000000054512845e+16, -6.000000083090567e+24, 2.4000002343777533e+33]
    Actual:
    [1.0, -100000000.0, 1.9999999999999996e+16, -5.999999999999999e+24, 2.4e+33]

The current implementation of `DivBackward0` could not calculate the results correctly even with `1e-8` for triple backward, even though the actual result still within the `float32` range.

See above.

[mfkasim1]: Those formulas are equal to each other.
The original formula is `-grad * self / (other * other)`, and I just substitute `self / other = result`, so it equals to `-grad * result / other`.
Another alternative is `-grad * (self / other) / other`, but it has more operations than the previous one.

[albanD]: Ho I didn't see the result change there!

However, when I use `-grad * (self / other) / other` formula, it can pass all the autograd tests successfully (same status with the previous implementation).
So now I think it is up to PyTorch's team to choose between:

1. `-grad * self / (other * other)`
2. `-grad * (self / other) / other`

The first one might be slightly faster (because the use of multiplication instead of division), but the second one provides better numerical stability.

[albanD]: > All of them are variables being modified inplace. I guess the formula -grad * result / other will introduce BC breaking.

title: PyTorch issue 43770
body:
I would like to suggest a small fix in the way that Python 3's exception chaining is used.

As described in detail in [this article](https://blog.ram.rachum.com/post/621791438475296768/improving-python-exception-chaining-with), exception chaining ([PEP 3134](https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-3134/)) can be used to make exceptions more user-friendly, and in that case, the syntax `raise new_exception from old_exception` needs to be used.

For example, the following should be used to chain exceptions:
```python
try:
    something_which_raises_TypeError
except TypeError as e:
    raise ValueError("A more user-friendly exception message.") from e
```
instead of:
```python
try:
    something_which_raises_TypeError
except TypeError:
    raise ValueError("A more user-friendly exception message.")
```

One example which needs to be fixed is:
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/c7787f7fbf388f9fe326d581726e7ef3f2dce74b/torch/jit/annotations.py#L32-L35

I'd be happy to PR! Let me know your thoughts on this!
comments:
[malfet]: Thank you for suggestion @akihironitta !
Please feel free to write a PR and I will be happy to review it.
Also consider eliminating all calls to that macro with direct `raise .. from ..` calls:
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/20abfc21e41dfe0bd2500295f7482edbeb6b6c05/torch/_six.py#L56-L60

Although not all instances require exception chaining, for example implicit chaining is totally fine in cases that you've mentioned in the issue description:
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/c7787f7fbf388f9fe326d581726e7ef3f2dce74b/torch/jit/annotations.py#L32-L35

---

[akihironitta]: Thank you for your quick response.

Sure, I'll remove `raise_from()` and use `raise .. from ..` instead all over the codebase.

> Although not all instances require exception chaining, for example implicit chaining is totally fine in cases that you've mentioned in the issue description:
> https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/c7787f7fbf388f9fe326d581726e7ef3f2dce74b/torch/jit/annotations.py#L32-L35

I agree that not all instances require exception chaining. However, I think we should not use implicit chaining in the above case because its error message `During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred` is confusing.

For example, if we run the script below (`test.py`):
```python
d = {"dog": 1}
key = "cat"
try: 
    print(d[key])  # raises KeyError
except KeyError:
    raise RuntimeError("no member called {}".format(key))
```
it'll give us an error message like this:
```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/nitta/tmp/test.py", line 4, in <module>
    print(d[key])  # raises KeyError
KeyError: 'cat'

During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/nitta/tmp/test.py", line 6, in <module>
    raise RuntimeError("no member called {}".format(key))
RuntimeError: no member called cat
```

`During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred` is somewhat confusing when debugging because the truth is that another exception occurred to explain the first exception (`KeyError` in this case) in a friendlier way, not because another **unexpected** exception occured while handling the first exception.

In order to fix confusing messages like this, one option is:
```python
try: 
    print(d[key])  # raises KeyError
except KeyError as e:
    raise RuntimeError("no member called {}".format(key)) from e
```
which outputs
```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/nitta/tmp/test.py", line 4, in <module>
    print(d[key])  # raises KeyError
KeyError: 'cat'

The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/nitta/tmp/test.py", line 6, in <module>
    raise RuntimeError("no member called {}".format(key)) from e
RuntimeError: no member called cat
```

However, in this case, the above message is a bit noisy and redundant.
If we want to suppress the first error message, we should use `raise .. from None` so as to suppress the first exception message (see [Suppress Context in PEP 3134](https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-3134/#open-issue-suppressing-context)).
```python
try: 
    print(d[key])  # raises KeyError
except KeyError:
    raise RuntimeError("no member called {}".format(key)) from None
```
which outputs
```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/nitta/tmp/test.py", line 6, in <module>
    raise RuntimeError("no member called {}".format(key)) from None
RuntimeError: no member called cat
```

Do you think using `raise .. from None` is reasonable in the below case or simliar cases?
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/c7787f7fbf388f9fe326d581726e7ef3f2dce74b/torch/jit/annotations.py#L32-L35

It can also make each PR relatively small. What do you think? (I can work on this issue by myself, but it might take some time...)~ I think I can handle this by myself.

title: PyTorch issue 44284
body:
After `nonzero` started warning that `as_tuple` is a required argument (1.6) a few unfortunate things has happened:
1) the examples in docs started issuing a warning #43425
2) there's no way to pass `out` and `as_tuple` arguments together
```
print(torch.nonzero(a, as_tuple=False)) #ok
print(torch.nonzero(a, out=out)) #warns
print(torch.nonzero(a, as_tuple=False, out=out)) #errors out with `TypeError: nonzero() received an invalid combination of arguments - got unrecognized keyword arguments: out`
```
The rationale behind making `as_tuple` argument required is going through deprecation cycle to change the default value of `as_tuple` so that `torch.nonzero` matches `numpy.nonzero` without any additional args. However, even if implemented properly without problems noted above, this goal is misguided and forces users to modify their codes to avoid warnings for no good reason. 
Torch default behavior for `nonzero` should not match numpy. Numpy behavior can already be achieved by either using `as_tuple=True` or calling `unbind(1)` on results of `torch.nonzero()` call, that is a very light burden for someone who wants it. But to avoid it, we are making everyone who doesn't care jump through deprecation hoops. 
Making numpy behavior default is bad, because numpy returns a tuple of tensors, whereas many users want single tensor return. Going from a single tensor to a tuple is a matter of a cheap `.unbind` call, going from a tuple to a single tensor is memory copy. Default behavior should always pick single tensor. 
My proposal is to go back to making `as_tuple` optional argument and not strive to make `nonzero` match numpy behavior.

## To Reproduce

2. Meanwhile, `lstsq` can also be solved in `scipy.linalg.lstsq`

Download files:

* `b.npy`: https://github.com/xiaosu-zhu/archives/releases/download/torch.lstsq/b.npy

```python

import scipy.linalg
import torch

# sparse 0-1 matrix with shape [100000, 1024]
# each row contains exactly 4 ones and other zeros
a = np.load("a.npy").astype(np.float32)
# int matrix with shape [100000, 128]
b = np.load("b.npy").astype(np.float32)

[chrisby]: In fact, I stumbled over the fact that you can reproduce this very easily with a 2 x 2 matrix:

```

Our team is currently working through linear algebra updates, but I've changed this issue to high priority. It should be fixed before the next release.

---

[xiaosu-zhu]: Thank you, @chrisby @mruberry. Look forward to the next release ❤️

---

[nikitaved]: The fix will probably require some thinking when it comes to handling rank-deficient inputs (which potentially leads to non-uniqueness). The current implementation is based on the LAPACK's [`?gels`](https://software.intel.com/content/www/us/en/develop/documentation/mkl-developer-reference-fortran/top/lapack-routines/lapack-least-squares-and-eigenvalue-problem-routines/lapack-least-squares-and-eigenvalue-problem-driver-routines/linear-least-squares-lls-problems-lapack-driver-routines/gels.html),
and the documentation reads that it expects the input of full rank.

@mruberry , is someone working on this one already?

---

[mruberry]: @nikitaved To the best of my knowledge no one is working on this.

---

[xiaosu-zhu]: Yes, the current implementation can't handle rank-deficient matrices, while [`scipy.linalg.lstsq`](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.linalg.lstsq.html) using three routines: [?gelss](https://software.intel.com/content/www/us/en/develop/documentation/mkl-developer-reference-fortran/top/lapack-routines/lapack-least-squares-and-eigenvalue-problem-routines/lapack-least-squares-and-eigenvalue-problem-driver-routines/linear-least-squares-lls-problems-lapack-driver-routines/gelss.html), [?gelsd](https://software.intel.com/content/www/us/en/develop/documentation/mkl-developer-reference-fortran/top/lapack-routines/lapack-least-squares-and-eigenvalue-problem-routines/lapack-least-squares-and-eigenvalue-problem-driver-routines/linear-least-squares-lls-problems-lapack-driver-routines/gelsd.html), [?gelsy](https://software.intel.com/content/www/us/en/develop/documentation/mkl-developer-reference-fortran/top/lapack-routines/lapack-least-squares-and-eigenvalue-problem-routines/lapack-least-squares-and-eigenvalue-problem-driver-routines/linear-least-squares-lls-problems-lapack-driver-routines/gelsy.html), also from LAPACK.

---

[nikitaved]: `?gelss, ?gelsd, ?gelsy` use SVD, but handle rand-deficient cases, while `?gels` does not use SVD, hence is faster, but does not handle rank-deficient cases.
Does it make sense to entirely switch to the SVD solution in `torch.linalg.lstsq`? Yes, we loose some speed, but at least we can avoid nasty errors during long trainings if the input becomes rank-deficient.

---

[mruberry]: Generally we should bias towards numerical correctness/stability/precision. However, in this case we don't have to decide one or the other. We can add an optional parameter to `linalg.lstsq` to select the current faster but less stable option.

---

[chrisby]: Yeah, this is exactly how `scipy` is doing it:

```
if driver is None:
    driver = lstsq.default_lapack_driver
if driver not in ('gelsd', 'gelsy', 'gelss'):
    raise ValueError('LAPACK driver "%s" is not found' % driver)
```

---

[nikitaved]: Well, for CUDA it seems like Magma has only `?gels` that works only for overdetermined matrices. Fear not, we can still use SVD/pseudo inverse for underdetermined/rank-deficient inputs in CUDA.

---

[nikitaved]: @mruberry , I have started working on this issue. The next release you mentioned above is 1.7.1, right?

[mruberry]: 1.7.1 is only some bugfixes for the 1.7 release. The next release from nightly is 1.8.

title: PyTorch issue 45821
body:
## 📚 Documentation

Now when `torch.svd` supports complex input both for CPU and CUDA. Let's discuss the docs.
Currently, SVD documentation is fully in agreement with the implementation. This function returns`(U, S, V)` such that `input = U @ diag(S) @ V.T`
However, the mathematical definition of SVD is the decomposition of a matrix **M** such that ![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/19621411/95017939-e72e4e80-0664-11eb-8efe-a853724d142a.png), where `V^*` is the conjugate transpose of `V`. 

What is the opinion on this? Should the documentation and implementation match math and be updated such that `A = U @ diag(S) @ V.T.conj()`?

[Link to `torch.svd` documentation](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.svd.html).



cc @ezyang @gchanan @zou3519 @bdhirsh @heitorschueroff @anjali411 @dylanbespalko @mruberry @jlin27 @vishwakftw @jianyuh @nikitaved @pearu @vincentqb
comments:
[pearu]: xref: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/45063 - conjugate transpose operator feature request

---

[pearu]: IIUC, the current SVD documentation uses transpose because previously only real input was supported (and hence using conjugate transpose would have been unnecessary). With the new complex input support in SVD, I would suggest updating the SVD documentation to use conjugate transpose to match the mathematical definition of general SVD. While doing so, also mention that when M is real then V will be real and conjugate transpose falls back to transpose.

---

[ezyang]: Yes, please just generalize the docs, in this case it seems to be straightforward and the right thing to do.

---

[nikitaved]: The current SVD implementation returns `V` that is silently conjugated. I guess it makes sense to fix that too, is that correct?

---

[mruberry]: > The current SVD implementation returns `V` that is silently conjugated. I guess it makes sense to fix that too, is that correct?

As far as I understand what you're saying: yes.

---

[antocuni]: I'd like to add my 2 cents to this discussion. By looking at the source code, it seems to me that the current behavior or `torch.svd` was not designed, but simply a byproduct of a bug. In particular, look at `_create_U_S_VT`:

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/a814231616f5db7fcdb8793f64c12d652d1e8572/aten/src/ATen/native/LinearAlgebraUtils.h#L221

As the name suggests, it should create a `VT` tensor, which is done here:
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/a814231616f5db7fcdb8793f64c12d652d1e8572/aten/src/ATen/native/LinearAlgebraUtils.h#L246-L247

However, the comment is wrong: the lapack's function `_gesdd` returns a `VT` in *column-major* order.

The rest of the code keeps calling it `VT`; e.g., this is `_svd_helper_cpu` returning a tuple `(U, S, VT)`:
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/a814231616f5db7fcdb8793f64c12d652d1e8572/aten/src/ATen/native/BatchLinearAlgebra.cpp#L1058

However, since we are creating the tensor with the wrong strides, we are effectively returning `VT.transpose()`, which is `V`. To summarize:
* `numpy.linalg.svd` returns `VT`
* lapack retusn `VT`
* our implementation returns something which is called `VT` (but it's not)

So, it looks to me that the intention was to return `VT` as well, but because of the bug in `_create_U_S_VT`, we started to return `V` and instead of fixing the bug we simply "fixed" the documentation.

There isn't much that we can to at this point without breaking compatibility, but this confusing/unexpected/nonstandard behavior of `svd` might indicate that we should deprecate it in favor or `torch.linalg.svd`, once it lands.

Note: in my WIP PR #45562 I fixed `_create_U_S_VT` by creating `VT` with the correct strides, and `transpose_()`ing it upon return to keep b/c.
In the same PR I am also going to fix the docs for `torch.svd`.

---

[mruberry]: Sounds great, @antocuni! I agree we should consider deprecating torch.svd once torch.linalg.svd lands. It will also be confusing to have a method torch.Tensor.svd when both functions are in because users may not know which svd it refers to.

---

[antocuni]: > It will also be confusing to have a method torch.Tensor.svd when both functions are in because users may not know which svd it refers to.

This is something which I didn't think about. What should `Tensor.svd` do if/when we remove `torch.svd`? Ideally it would do the same as `torch.linalg.svd`, but this will break compatibility.

> In the same PR I am also going to fix the docs for torch.svd.

FWIW, this is the commit which aims to fix the documentation:
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/45562/commits/97662da54aba366dd547e46d557edc2b86ff86dc

---

[mruberry]: > > It will also be confusing to have a method torch.Tensor.svd when both functions are in because users may not know which svd it refers to.
> 
> This is something which I didn't think about. What should `Tensor.svd` do if/when we remove `torch.svd`? Ideally it would do the same as `torch.linalg.svd`, but this will break compatibility.

We should warn/deprecate for a release and then remove both functions for a release. Then we can consider adding torch.Tensor.svd back and mapping it to torch.linalg.svd.

---

[antocuni]: (sorry guys, I closed the issue by mistake, reopening it)

---

[pulkin]: You probably do know that `numpy` returns `u, s, vh = svd(A)` such that `A = u @ s @ vh`. I would prefer to have this convention in `pytorch` because many people use `numpy` for prototyping.

---

[antocuni]: while working on PR #45562 we realized that we can't fix `torch.svd` without breaking existing code. OTOH, the upcoming `torch.linalg.svd` is completely compatible with numpy.
As discussed on the PR, the current plan is to document the current behavior of `torch.svd` and tell people to use `torch.linalg.svd` for new code: this is the commit which tentatively tries to improve the docs, but feel free to suggest a better wording:

## 🐛 Bug

In one of the `transformers` tests `torch.save` w/ the new `_use_new_zipfile_serialization=True` corrupts the data in the state_dict resulting in load returning bogus data that wasn't there on save. 

## To Reproduce

Steps to reproduce the behavior:

It seems to happen with the specific data only, so at the moment requires a specific sub-test:
```
git clone https://github.com/huggingface/transformers
cd transformers
pip install -e .[dev]
CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1 USE_CUDA=1 pytest tests/test_modeling_bert.py::BertModelTest::test_head_pruning_integration

Specifically, we have https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/960faaaf28b198c0dd2fcb288fa336a846aed398/src/transformers/modeling_utils.py#L729

        torch.save(state_dict, output_model_file) #, _use_new_zipfile_serialization=False)

        if k in state_dict: print("SAVE\n", state_dict[k])

        state_dict = torch.load(output_model_file)
        if k in state_dict: print("LOAD\n", state_dict[k])
```

These 2 peculiarities are very odd. Is there a race condition here and somehow one or the other changes the timing?

## 🐛 Bug

The cuSOLVER path in `torch.inverse` seems not to raise an error for non-invertible input.

## To Reproduce

Single matrix and 2xNxN batched input inversion is based on cuSOLVER

A = A.reshape((1, 3, 3))
A = A.repeat(batch_dim, 1, 1)
A[0, -1, -1] = 0  # Now A[0] is singular
Ainv = torch.inverse(A) # Raises RuntimeError because input is singular
```

<!-- If you have a code sample, error messages, stack traces, please provide it here as well -->

`torch.inverse` should raise an error for singular input when input is single matrix or a batch of matrices with batch size less or equal than 2 (cuSOLVER's code path).

title: PyTorch issue 46561
body:
## 🐛 Bug

On process group initialisation failure the global variable `torch.distributed.distributed_c10d._group_count` can be incremented by one even though no process group is created. This is because the counter is incremented at the beginning of `_new_process_group_helper` (https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/distributed/distributed_c10d.py#L491) while the other global variables are set at the end.

This matters because depending on the crashing and recovery process the variable may end up taking a different value for different processes. And since the counter is used as a prefix for the `PrefixStore` the processes will be using different keys, leading to a socket timeout.

This issue cannot be "correctly" prevented since `_group_count` is private and `destroy_process_group` cannot be called here since the process group doesn't exist. It can be prevented by explicitly providing a group name to `init_process_group`, but the argument is marked as deprecated.

## To Reproduce

The following code :

```
import torch.distributed.distributed_c10d as c10d
import datetime

def print_global_vars():
    print("===========")
    print("_pg_map", c10d._pg_map)
    print("_pg_names", c10d._pg_names)
    print("_pg_group_ranks", c10d._pg_group_ranks)
    print("_default_pg", c10d._default_pg)
    print("_default_pg_init_method", c10d._default_pg_init_method)
    print("_group_count", c10d._group_count)

print_global_vars()
try:
    c10d.init_process_group("gloo", timeout=datetime.timedelta(milliseconds=1), rank=0, world_size=2, init_method=f"tcp://127.0.0.1:8000")
except RuntimeError:
    pass

print_global_vars()
```

This shows the following output:

```
===========
_pg_map {}
_pg_names {}
_pg_group_ranks {}
_default_pg None
_default_pg_init_method None
_group_count 0
===========
_pg_map {}
_pg_names {}
_pg_group_ranks {}
_default_pg None
_default_pg_init_method None
_group_count 1
```

## Expected behavior

It should be possible to recover from a failed call to `init_process_group` with public methods such as `is_initialized` and `destroy_process_group`. In the current implementation this means the call should leave the global variables in a consistent state, i.e. either none or all of them should be modified. In the above example, `_group_count` should remain at zero.

```

## Additional context

This issue happens in an elastic training training context where the main process group is frequently reinitialised, and there is a rare crash where the initialisation fails due to a broken pairwise connection. I am unsure if this is due to a networking error or a bug in the code, but the above issue makes it difficult to recover from the crash. This is in part because some of the processes crash in `ProcessGroupGloo.__init__`,  leading to inconsistent state, while others crash in the `barrier()` call at the end of `init_process_group`. The recovery process is roughly as follow:
```
while True:
    try:
        torch.distributed.init_process_group(...)
        break
    except Exception:
        if torch.distributed.is_initialized():
            torch.distributed.destroy_process_group()
```
But `_group_count` can be different across processes, so the recovery won't work.

title: PyTorch issue 46585
body:
**1)** nn.Embedding documentation says:

> padding_idx (int, optional): If given, pads the output with the embedding vector at :attr:`padding_idx`
>                                          **(initialized to zeros)** whenever it encounters the index.

But, In case of using the `from_pretrained` version, if input is equal to padding_idx, weigths[padding_idx] gets returned and not a vector of zeros.

Code example for reproducing:
```python
predefined_weights = torch.rand(10, 3)
emb = torch.nn.Embedding.from_pretrained(embeddings=predefined_weights, padding_idx=0)
result = emb(torch.LongTensor([1,2,0]))
```
The 3rd vector in the result is not a zero vector.

This might be a documentation issue, and the doc should say that in case of using `from_pretrained`, padding_idx will not return a zero vector, but instead, weigths[padding_idx]
**But**, it makes the use of `padding_idx` in `from_pretrained` redundant, thus I would suggest removing `padding_idx` from the arguments if this is indeed the case.

I can open a PR for this but need some feedback regarding the approach to take here, please advise.

**2)** nn.**functional**.embedding documentation says:
 

> padding_idx (int, optional): If given, pads the output with the embedding vector at :attr:`padding_idx`
>                                          (**initialized to zeros**) whenever it encounters the index.

But, the result for `index = padding_idx`  returns weigths[padding_idx] and not a zero vector.

Code example for reproducing:
```python
predefined_weights = torch.rand(10, 3)
result = torch.nn.functional.embedding(torch.LongTensor([1,2,0]), predefined_weights, padding_idx=0)
```
The 3rd vector in the result is not a zero vector.

IMO this is a documentation issue, and the doc should say that padding_idx pads the output with the embedding vector at padding_idx. (and not a zero vector)

The names prefixed with an underscore are meant to be private (a convention) and it's fine to have them undocumented. To pass the user-defined weight matrix, use `nn.Embedding.from_pretrained(...)`. The `_weights` param are used internally for this purpose.

@skipIf(not torch.cuda.is_available())

@filterwarnings("ignore:CUDA initialization.*:UserWarning")

    ...

@skipIf(not torch.cuda.is_available())

title: PyTorch issue 47449
body:
## 🐛 Bug
Tensors of different shapes can be considered `allclose`:
```python
import torch

# Two tensors of different shapes
A = torch.zeros((1, 1))
B = torch.zeros((1,))

torch.testing.assert_allclose(A, B) # passes
```

## Expected behavior

The numpy equivalent - which `assert_allclose` [was based on](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/6200) - fails, as it should:
```python
import numpy as np

A = np.zeros((1, 1))
B = np.zeros((1,))

np.testing.assert_allclose(A, B) # fails
```

```

## Additional context
The culprit is these two lines
```python
    if expected.shape != actual.shape:
        expected = expected.expand_as(actual)
```
in `assert_allclose`. This means it's obviously deliberate that shape's ignored, but the divergence from numpy is surprising. What's even more surprising is that it makes `assert_allclose` noncommutative:

torch.testing.assert_allclose(A, B) # passes
torch.testing.assert_allclose(B, A) # fails

title: PyTorch issue 47629
body:
## 🐛 Bug

Possible root cause for https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/45435.  CC @walterddr 
Thanks to @jaglinux for the following triage information.

For barrier call, all reduce uses tensor of device type cuda with the following formula:

`int16_t deviceIdx = static_cast<int16_t>(rank_ % numGPUs);`

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/a49367e9c9fcfa9547782420a24441f13fef19dc/torch/lib/c10d/ProcessGroupNCCL.cpp#L1413

But when the tests are called, the tensors uses different formula to calculate rank to GPU selection.

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/a49367e9c9fcfa9547782420a24441f13fef19dc/torch/testing/_internal/distributed/distributed_test.py#L367-L374

Hence for rank 0,1,2 ; barrier uses tensors of cuda0, cuda1, cuda2 device type and for testing, tensors of cuda0, cuda2, cuda4 are used.

If we change `rank_to_GPU` data structure in distributed_test.py to return `rank % numGPUs`. With this change, all the tests are passing.

cc @pietern @mrshenli @pritamdamania87 @zhaojuanmao @satgera @rohan-varma @gqchen @aazzolini @xush6528 @osalpekar @jiayisuse @agolynski @SciPioneer @H-Huang @mrzzd

[jaglinux]: I was running the python test_distributed_spawn tests on a 8 gpu machine with rank as 3. All the tests belonging to default group testing (group.WORLD) were failing due to timeout. Reason is rank to gpu mapping is different in  barrier and distributed_test.py.
Issue does not happen in new groups because it uses nccl new stream for the test run (after barrier call).
Quick fix is to mimic the rank % numGPUs behavior in distributed_test.py rank_to_GPU.
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/a49367e9c9fcfa9547782420a24441f13fef19dc/torch/testing/_internal/distributed/distributed_test.py#L367-L374

--- a/torch/testing/_internal/distributed/distributed_test.py
+++ b/torch/testing/_internal/distributed/distributed_test.py
@@ -364,7 +364,7 @@ class DistributedTest:
```
             if BACKEND == "nccl":
                 apply_hack_for_nccl()

-            nGPUs_per_process = nGPUs // world_size
+            nGPUs_per_process = 1

             rank_to_GPU = {
                 i: list(
                     visible_devices[i * nGPUs_per_process: (i + 1) * nGPUs_per_process]
```

Long term fix could be adding a new function parameter to specify tensor in barrier() for nccl backend.
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/a49367e9c9fcfa9547782420a24441f13fef19dc/torch/lib/c10d/ProcessGroupNCCL.cpp#L1403

body:
## 🐛 Bug

observation: pytorch native amp consumes 10x memory as compared to fp16/apex or no `--fp16` usage.

The issue has been originally discovered and tracked at https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/issues/8403 and on slack, but now we know for sure that this is a pytorch issue, so let's concentrate the discussion here.

## To Reproduce

What's following is the minimal script that was reduced from a rather complex logic of `finetune.py` in `transformers`. It originates in a complex stack of `pytorch-lightning` feeding `transformers` generate/beam_search logic finally feeding to real pytorch logic in `BartForConditionalGeneration`. If you want to see the full blow up and how to set it up, it's described [here](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/issues/8403).

I found at least part of the culprit or trigger of the leak - it's `@torch.no_grad()` used for `generate` https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/eb3bd73ce35bfef56eeb722d697f2d39a06a8f8d/src/transformers/generation_utils.py#L281-L282

Here is a short script that reproduces the leakage. It removes all the generate/search logic and feeds the same random `input_ids` to `BartForConditionalGeneration` pre-trained model.

Please first run:
```
pip install ipyexperiments 
```
to get the memory tracing, but feel free to disable it if for some reason it's not working for you and use some alternative like `nvidia-smi` dumping. (but it should work)

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python

import os
import sys
import torch
os.environ["USE_TF"] = "0"
sys.path.insert(1, "src")

# !pip install ipyexperiments 
from ipyexperiments.utils.mem import gpu_mem_get_used_mbs, gpu_mem_get_used_no_cache_mbs

from transformers import BartForConditionalGeneration

device = torch.device('cuda:0' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu')

model = BartForConditionalGeneration.from_pretrained('sshleifer/student_cnn_12_6').to(device)
model.eval()

vocab_size = 50264 # model.config.vocab_size
length = 10

AUTOCAST = False if "-f" in sys.argv else True
print(f"autocast: {AUTOCAST}")

class MemReport():
    def __init__(self, gc_collect=True):
        self.get_mem = gpu_mem_get_used_no_cache_mbs if gc_collect else gpu_mem_get_used_mbs
        self.cur = self.get_mem()
    def delta(self, id):
        peak = torch.cuda.memory_stats()["allocated_bytes.all.peak"]
        print(f"{id}: {gpu_mem_get_used_mbs()-self.cur}MB (peak {peak>>20}MB)")
        self.cur = self.get_mem()
        
mr = MemReport(gc_collect=False)

### reproducible code starts here ###

@torch.no_grad()
def logic():
    input_ids = torch.randint(vocab_size, (1,length)).to(device)
    mr.delta(0)
    for i in range(1,10):
        outputs = model(input_ids)
        mr.delta(i)

if AUTOCAST:
    with torch.cuda.amp.autocast():
        logic()
else:
    logic()
```

So if I run it with `-f` which disables `autocast`, I get:

```

You can see that we are leaking 600Mb per forward call here.

If I comment out `@torch.no_grad()`, the total memory usage doubles but there is no leak:

comments:
[ezyang]: I read through the downstream discussion. I agree that there are (multiple) legitimate bugs; but furthermore, I think we were wrong to close earlier reports that AMP leaks memory when you use AMP outside of your training loop. This should work. @mcarilli, I'll try to explain why below.

On its face, it would make sense that a cache that only gets cleared when you exit AMP would leak memory over time. But AMP only caches casts on parameters: you should be using the same parameters in each loop of the training loop (and updating them in place). What is there to leak? In fact, there should be no leak, and instead we have a correctness bug where we will improperly use casts even when the original parameters have been updated. We ought to fix that.

But let's suppose that, somehow, you're generating fresh new parameters every iteration of the loop. Those parameters are ostensibly going dead when you go around the loop, and so if we implemented a weak map correctly, they should still get pruned anyway. Well I looked over the code and there are still some problems:

* We don't seem to ever traverse the map to get rid of dead entries, where the key is dead. This is a big deal because even though the source parameter's data gets deallocated when it becomes dead, the *cached cast output* doesn't get deallocated unless you remove it from the map. So the weak pointer is only solving half the problem: we prevented the source parameter from getting leaked, but we're still leaking the cached output.
* I stared at the code some more and I got worried about another possible memory leak: the cached output cast has a `grad_fn` that will refer to the parameter via a grad accumulator. I now don't remember if this is a weak reference or a strong ref; if it's strong, that's a reference cycle and would also prevent the weak pointer key from ever getting collected either.

We probably didn't notice any of this because it's mostly OK to just leak everything until the end of one step in the training loop... except in situations like this.

PS. I'm kind of sad we don't live in a GC'ed language, as a lot of this weak pointer/map business gets a lot simpler if you can assume there's some GC process that will clean up after you.

btw, cc @swolchok, this is an example of weak pointers actually being important for tensors

---

[agolynski]: @mcarilli

---

[mcarilli]: I was still confused because https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/aten/src/ATen/autocast_mode.cpp#L71 should ensure the only things that get cached are leaves (model params) that require grad.  These don't move between iterations of the loop under `no_grad`.  @ptrblck investigated yesterday in depth yesterday and we realized there are 3 ingredients that cause the cache blowup we didn't discuss so far:
1. All tensors created in a `no_grad` context are considered leaves, because they don't have autograd history.
2. Linear layers don't send their weights directly to the matmul call, rather, they send [`weight.t()`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/9b526546202cf53c90ed3a438c16260386475680/torch/nn/functional.py#L1665-L1667), which is a new Tensor (with a new TensorImpl) each time.  (further unfortunate consequence:  this means without `no_grad`, the cache was doing nothing for linear layers, because it never saw incoming `weight.t()`s as leaves.)
3. View ops (like `t()`) in `no_grad` context _do_ propagate requires_gradness from their source tensor.

With 1, 2, and 3 together, when `forward` with many linear layers is called in a loop under `no_grad`, in every matmul in every iteration `cached_cast` sees incoming weights as leaves that require grad and have a new TensorImpl, so it creates a new cache entry with a new fp16 copy every time.

The plot thickens, though.  3. is an _inconsistent behavior_ between view ops and out-of-place ops in `no_grad` contexts.  View ops propagate requires_gradness of the source, ordinary out-of-place ops don't:
```python
with torch.no_grad():
    print(a.requires_grad) # True
    b = a.clone()
    print(b.requires_grad) # False
    b = a.t()
    print(b.requires_grad) # True
    b = a.view(-1)
    print(b.requires_grad) # True
```
This may be due to some short-circuiting in view ops, I haven't looked in detail.
@albanD , is the above behavior expected, or a bug?  Seems like a bug to me: since view ops do create distinct tensors, they should have the same source-tensor-attribute-propagation policy as out-of-place ops.  But maybe the different policy is a deliberate choice for some reason I don't get.

One option:  If we changed view ops to _not_ propagate requires_gradness under `no_grad` (consistent with the behavior of out-of-place ops) it would fix the cache blowup, because the incoming `weight.t()`s would have `requires_grad=False`, therefore `cached_cast` would not try to cache their casts.  It wouldn't be ideal because it would defeat the purpose of caching, but it would be no worse than running without `no_grad` (see "2....further unfortunate consequence")

---

[t-vi]: The special handling of views in `no_grad` is required, this is part of `DifferentiableViewMeta` in `torch/csrc/autograd/variable.h`:

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/98fddc1f061fb5b0dcac9f49b3b096bcdc124a12/torch/csrc/autograd/variable.h#L322-L337

I think checking `t._base()` to detect non-leaves to handle that case could eliminate 1.

---

[albanD]: Yes views need to inherit the requires grad from their base otherwise code like the following would not work
```python
base = torch.rand(1, 5)
slice1 = base[0]
slice2 = base[0]

# This makes slice1 and base properly require gradients
slice1.copy_(torch.rand(5, requires_grad=True))
# Other views need to also be properly updated by reading the base's status
loss = slice2.sum()
loss.backward()
```


Do I understand properly that the issue is that this view op makes it so that the input to the linear (and thus your cache) is different at each iteration and so a new entry is created every time (and never cleaned up even when the Tensor goes out of scope)?

---

[mcarilli]: @albanD thanks for the thorough analysis!  i need some time to digest it all :P but it sounds like we can fix the main issue without waiting for my brain to catch up.

> I think checking t._base() to detect non-leaves to handle that case could eliminate 1.

Are you proposing we check `t._base()` somehow in the line where we check for cache eligibility (https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/aten/src/ATen/autocast_mode.cpp#L71)?

---

[albanD]: I guess you could check `!t.is_view()` there indeed. If you say that you never want to cache the result for a view of a larger Tensor?
But then what happens if someone actually have weights that are views of a bigger Tensor for some reason? The caching will just miss them completely.
So I don't think you can have something that will work for everything here by just looking at the Tensor. But maybe never caching views will be a good enough heuristic.

---

[ezyang]: Thanks, this is a good analysis. A quick thoughts: view cache blow up due to .t() can be solved with a simple heuristic: if we have a view of a parameter, cast the *source* of the view and cache that. Then, when checking the cache, if we are given a view, check if we have a cache of the view base, and if so, redo the view on top of that.

---

[albanD]: Users might have the bad idea to assign as a parameter a small slice of a much bigger Tensor. Such approach would process a very big Tensor that should not be be processed.
But this would be rare as well.

---

[ezyang]: If this is a concern, you can update the heuristic to only see through view operations that preserve numel.

Also, it is only a problem to cast the bigger tensor *if you don't actually use the rest of the parameters in the bigger tensor in that run*. If you do use them, then you probably are going to autocast them too, in which case you're just paying for it up front.

---

[mcarilli]: > update the heuristic to only see through view operations that preserve numel.

I like this idea, but I don't think it should block https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/48696, which is a simple fix that's strictly better than current code.

---

[stas00]: May I also ask in this context why caching is skipped if: `!arg.requires_grad()` - e.g. multple transformers models have static positional embedding (not part of the grad tree) which don't ever change so I'd think those should be cached.

And moreover, since they don't ever change these would be a candidate for a constant cache and not re-calculated on each enter/exit from autocast context (if memory allows for that luxury).

Unless there is a way to force tensors to have both float and half values on the user side if the user knows that it'd be beneficial to have those converted values cached once.

I don't know whether there has been a discussion about a session-level cache.

---

[mcarilli]: > May I also ask in this context why caching is skipped if: !arg.requires_grad()

@stas00  `is_leaf()`, as far as I know, checks if the tensor has any autograd history (@albanD knows more).  If we're not under no_grad, you're probably right:  `arg.is_leaf()` suffices to tell us if an incoming param is a static model param in most cases.

But if we are under no_grad, all newly created tensors pass the `arg.is_leaf()` check, because they don't have autograd history.  If we get rid of the `arg.requires_grad()` check, all fp32->fp16 casts for such internal temporaries will be cached, more such temporaries will be cached every iteration of the `forward` loop, and we have another cache blowup.  In this way, under no_grad the `arg.requires_grad()` check is the best way of ensuring we only cache casts for the true static model params, because most** of the temporaries will have `arg.requires_grad() == false` and be ineligible for caching.  It's not a perfect heuristic but I'm not sure how we can make it perfect.  The only information `cached_cast` has is `is_leaf()`, `requires_grad()`, and `is_view()`, and with those it needs to make its best guess whether to cache or not (while hopefully avoiding blowups in calling code).

** the exception is view temporaries like `weight.t()`, which _do_ inherit requires_grad-ness from their parents, so they passed both the is_leaf() and requires_grad() checks to cause the original blowup.

---

[stas00]: Thank you for the detailed explanation, @mcarilli. 

Following this discussion it sounds like the main problem here is that there is an expectation that `autocast` is supposed to magically optimize everything - and everything is different, so as you all have been saying this is an impossible task, and battles have to be picked.

Would the developers consider adding some manual options in addition to the magical `autocast`. For example, could a tensor have a flag that will make it cachable unconditionally?

For example for static positional embeddings we already call `detach` and turn grads off, so we could just as well turn on a hypothetical "cache-these-weights-if-under-fp16" flag. And then another flag for the caching scope `{autocast|session}` - so the tensor will still get cached under `autocast` even if normal conditions for caching won't apply.  And in the case of the `session` scope `autocast` will not release these at the end of its scope.

This is a half-baked idea since I haven't measured the actual impact and the importance of such need. But perhaps some of you who have a lot more practical experience can think of situations where being able to manually control such caching would lead to a faster program at a reasonable memory cost and no memory leaking. I could be wrong and perhaps such need is very minor and is not worthy the added complexity.

So this is not a request but just an idea that I'm asking whether it is reasonable/useful/worthy consideration.

Thank you.

title: PyTorch issue 48666
body:
## 🐛 Bug

Using the DataLoader causes the main process to hang on exit waiting to join the indices queue putting thread when the sampler is large (e.g., when `batch_size` is large) and a reference to the iterator is kept around (e.g., when `persistent_workers=True`). For instance, see the following simple script:

```py
import torch

class Dataset(torch.utils.data.Dataset):
    def __len__(self):
        return 10000000

    def __getitem__(self, any):
        return torch.empty(0)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    dl = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(
        Dataset(),
        batch_size=40960,
        num_workers=1)

    it = iter(dl)

    for i, x in enumerate(it):
        print(x.shape)
        raise RuntimeError()
```

Running the above in the below environment (pretty standard) will hang at exiting. Some probing suggests that this is due to the main process try to join the `_index_queues`. And, **due to** the iterator being around, the ordering of python atexit calls decides to call the `multiprocessing.Queue` clean-up (which joins the queue putting thread) before cleaning up `_MultiprocessingDataLoaderIter.__del__` (which would clean-up nicely). 

Finally, since the above uses a sampler with *large* indices sent to workers at each time (constructed by the dataloader using a `RandomSampler` wrapped in a `BatchSampler`), the putting thread is hanging waiting for more room in the pipe. The stderr will hang at 
```py
torch.Size([40960, 0])
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "XXXX/test.py", line 34, in <module>
    raise RuntimeError()
RuntimeError
```

NB: the worker yields empty tensors, and thus its putter thread shouldn't be the reason of hanging.


To confirm that this also happens with a simpler sampler, the following script with disabled auto-batching hangs similarly:
```py
import torch


class BigSampler(object):
    def __iter__(self):
        for idx in range(20):
            yield [idx for idx in range(40960)]


class Dataset(torch.utils.data.Dataset):

    def __init__(self):
        self.first_time = True

    def __len__(self):
        return 10000000

    def __getitem__(self, indices):
        # NB: this is called *once* per dataloader fetch since we disabled auto-batching!
        if not self.first_time:
            # simulate some work so that the index_queue is likely non-empty 
            # (and thus the main process's queue putting is waiting). 
            import time
            time.sleep(0.1)
        self.first_time = False
        return torch.empty(0)


if __name__ == '__main__':
    dl = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(
        Dataset(),
        batch_size=None,
        sampler=BigSampler(),
        num_workers=1)

    it = iter(dl)

    for i, x in enumerate(it):
        print(x.shape)
        raise RuntimeError()
```

title: PyTorch issue 48874
body:
This check https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/e7ca62be08f96b07efc1271baf9b02d4e7be226a/cmake/Modules/FindARM.cmake#L44-L45 prevents an Apple Silicon Mac from building an x86_64 variant of Pytorch.

I'm sure the check exists because folks are installing CMake as an x86_64 binary from homebrew, so they want to use it to pick a different architecture from the CMake architecture, however this is how I got here:

I built and installed both CMake and ninja as Universal 2 binaries.
I built Python 3.9.1rc1 as x86_64 using `arch -x86_64`  before the Python configure/make commands.

When I run this x86_64 Python, it runs the x86_64 CMake binary, which is actually correct in this case (unlike the case where you only have an x86_64 CMake binary, so arm64 processes drop to x86_64 and you need the sysctl).

With `CMAKE_SYSTEM_PROCESSOR=x86_64 CMAKE_OSX_ARCHITECTURES=x86_64 python3.9 setup.py build` and a small fix to CMake itself (upstream issue here https://gitlab.kitware.com/cmake/cmake/-/issues/21554), I am able to convince Pytorch to build as x86_64 on this machine.

However, it breaks partway through the build due to the NEON definitions that are enabled by the issue I'm describing here.

If I remove the sysctl check in FindARM, an x86_64 build completes successfully on an M1, which I was able to manually `lipo` to make a fully universal2 pytorch package.

title: PyTorch issue 49998
body:
## 🐛 Bug

As explained in [this forum thread](https://discuss.pytorch.org/t/how-does-torch-normal-work-with-a-negative-standard-deviation/107571/3) torch.normal only gives an error for negative sigma when there is no size argument given in. Code examples are below.

## To Reproduce

Steps to reproduce the behavior:

This code cause an error...

```
torch.manual_seed(8)
torch.normal(0, -1, (10, ))

# output
# RuntimeError                              Traceback (most recent call last)
# <ipython-input-6-f3bb1e6c1119> in <module>()
    #   1 torch.manual_seed(8)
# ----> 2 torch.normal(0, -1, (10, ))

# RuntimeError: normal_ expects std > 0.0, but found std=-1
```

while this code causes no error...

```
mu = torch.tensor(0.0)
sigma = torch.tensor(-3.0)
torch.normal(mu, sigma)

# ...output
>>> torch.normal(mu, sigma)
tensor(-3.6977)
>>> torch.normal(mu, sigma)
tensor(-3.0448)
>>> torch.normal(mu, sigma)
tensor(-0.2327)
```

<!-- If you have a code sample, error messages, stack traces, please provide it here as well -->

## Expected behavior

I would expect that the error reporting would be consistent and that a negative standard deviation on a singleton sample would also give an error.

## Environment

Please copy and paste the output from our
[environment collection script](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pytorch/pytorch/master/torch/utils/collect_env.py)
(or fill out the checklist below manually).

You can get the script and run it with:
```

python collect_env.py
```

comments:
[ngimel]: Thanks for reporting, it's a bug. The problematic functions are here https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/e44b2b72bd4ccecf9c2f6c18d09c11eff446b5a3/aten/src/ATen/native/DistributionTemplates.h#L219-L249, they don't check that std is positive. 
High pri for silent correctness, however, checking if std is valid is a perf penalty, we should discuss if we want it.

---

[jeffwillette]: As I said in the forum thread I came across this bug in a repository where the user had no positive condition such as training the parameter in the log-space or using a softplus. I was confused as to why their code was working and more confused when I saw no error in Pytorch. 

I would strongly side in favor of checking even if there is a performance penalty because it is:

- very confusing that it fails only with the size argument
- silently works even though the user may be totally wrong in the way that they call it.

---

[mruberry]: We would accept a PR fixing this on CPU. We're OK with checking the values of the tensor and paying the performance penalty on CPU. We should document this is validated on CPU but not on CUDA. 

Note for the future: it would be interesting to investigate adding a CUDA assert for CUDA.

---

[gchanan]: @ngimel argued we can't (easily) on-device assert TensorIterator because our lambdas aren't complicated/smart enough.  It would be good to figure out how difficult it would be to do this.

---

[jeffwillette]: I do not think it would be a good idea to add another inconsistent behavior on top of an existing one. If it can't be synced across CPU/CUDA. Would it be better to just document that a single sample (without size arg) does not enforce a positive sigma constraint?

---

[fritzo]: (removing `module: distributions` label because the `distributions.Normal` wrapper already checks for negative sigma)

---

[ousou]: I noticed that the same error is present in PyTorch version 1.7.1 also when using the distributions.Normal wrapper. This makes the log_prob function return NaN on any value:

```
>>> a = torch.distributions.Normal(0,-1)
>>> a.log_prob(0)
tensor(nan)
>>> a.log_prob(1)
tensor(nan)
>>> a.log_prob(0.5)
tensor(nan)
>>> a.log_prob(-0.5)
tensor(nan)
```

---

[kshitij12345]: @ousou Looks to be fixed in master. Can you try nightly

```python
>>> a = torch.distributions.Normal(0,-1)
ValueError: The parameter scale has invalid values
```

---

[kurtamohler]: This issue was fixed by #51317, apparently I didn't link it to auto close.

---

[pjh4993]: I found that during training model, gradient can change sigma to negative
Is that not bug and responsibility to check for negative sigma is for user?

---

[kurtamohler]: If the gradient calculation is changing sigma, that seems like an issue. The backward functions for `torch.normal` should only be setting gradients to zero, so sigma (called `std` here) shouldn't change: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/056a8e0d5cc6b53dd574b77eebf273ded646f81e/tools/autograd/derivatives.yaml#L1051-L1062

Do you have a reproducer script @pjh4993?

---

[jkbh]: I was wondering why the behaviour was changed from requiring std < 0 to std <= 0. The normal distrbution is not defined for std=0 and I think this can still lead to silent correctness and unexpectedly working code.

---

[kurtamohler]: @jkbh, I'm not a math expert by any means, so I don't know any of the formalism behind this. But as the standard deviation of a normal distribution approaches 0, the range of possible outputs shrinks to include only the mean of the distribution. Numpy does this as well:

```python
>>> import numpy as np
>>> import torch
>>> np.random.normal(loc=1, scale=0, size=())
array(1.)
>>> torch.normal(mean=1, std=0, size=())
tensor(1.)
```

Maybe someone else here can give a more rigorous explanation than me

title: PyTorch issue 50064
body:
As of #36377, min/max functions were disabled for complex inputs (via dtype checks), however, min/max kernels are still compiled and dispatched for complex, see e.g.  
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/e44b2b72bd4ccecf9c2f6c18d09c11eff446b5a3/aten/src/ATen/native/cpu/ReduceAllOpsKernel.cpp#L77
This dispatch should be disabled, and we should rely on errors produced by dispatch macro to not run those ops on complex, instead of doing redundant dtype checks.

cc @t-vi, thanks for reporting!

[ngimel]: Reopening. The linked PR only disables dispatch on cpu reductions, it does not handle pointwise operations, and it does not handle cuda operations. 
I also asked for redundant type checks to be removed (because dispatch would produce necessary error messages), and they are still in place.

---

[imaginary-person]: > Reopening. The linked PR only disables dispatch on cpu reductions, it does not handle pointwise operations, and it does not handle cuda operations.
> I also asked for redundant type checks to be removed (because dispatch would produce necessary error messages), and they are still in place.

Hello @ngimel, Sorry about that! l had realized that I hadn't disabled the type-checks introduced in #36377, after Richard suggested writing a test, and I recently submitted another PR (#50465). For CPU min/max  ops in TensorCompareKernel.cpp, I had skipped it by mistake due to some confusion between the names of `max_stub` & `maximum_stub`. So, I changed them in this PR.


As for the  CUDA operations, their kernels do not seem to be compiled & dispatched for complex types anyway, so I think that no further changes are required. Please confirm if my rationale is correct. Thanks!

Basically, the dispatch macros currently being used don't have cases (of switch statements) for complex types, so they'd default to error for complex types.
For example, 

1. the reduce CUDA ops use [AT_DISPATCH_ALL_TYPES_AND2](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/aten/src/ATen/Dispatch.h#L548-L575) in [ReduceMinMaxKernel.cu](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/ReduceMinMaxKernel.cu), and that macro doesn't allow complex types.

2. In [MinMaxElementwiseKernel.cu](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/MaxMinElementwiseKernel.cu), the CUDA pointwise ops use [AT_DISPATCH_FLOATING_TYPES_AND2](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/aten/src/ATen/Dispatch.h#L240-L263) for non-integral & non-boolean types, and this marco doesn't have a case for complex types either.

---

[imaginary-person]: **Duplicate comment from #50465 for the convenience of any potential readers in the future. Please skip if you read the PR #50465.**

There are a few cases in which the methods corresponding to `min_stub()` or `max_stub()` are not called, so dispatch macros don't get invoked, resulting in no exceptions being raised. Hence, `dtype` checks are necessary at 3 places:

1. https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/52dcc7299925de055d330781d2fe0dad71182829/aten/src/ATen/native/TensorCompare.cpp#L342
2. https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/52dcc7299925de055d330781d2fe0dad71182829/aten/src/ATen/native/TensorCompare.cpp#L422
3. https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/52dcc7299925de055d330781d2fe0dad71182829/aten/src/ATen/native/TensorCompare.cpp#L389

The first dtype check requirement can be verified from the following example Python code:
```
import unittest 
import torch

class MyTestCase(unittest.TestCase): 
  
   def test_1(self):
      t = torch.tensor((1 + 1j), device='cpu', dtype=torch.complex128) 
      with self.assertRaises(RuntimeError): 
         torch.max(t, dim=0)
  
if __name__ == '__main__':  
    unittest.main()
```

[ltrottier]: #### Solution (torch >= 0.4)

This is my solution:

1. First, reset the numpy seed at the beginning of each epoch:

```python
for epoch in range(2):
    print("epoch {}".format(epoch))
    np.random.seed() # reset seed
    for batch in ds:
        print(batch)
```

2. Use `worker_init_fn` to set the numpy seed of each worker:
```python
def worker_init_fn(worker_id):                                                          
    np.random.seed(np.random.get_state()[1][0] + worker_id)

ds = RandomDataset()
ds = DataLoader(ds, 10, shuffle=False, num_workers=4, worker_init_fn=worker_init_fn)
```

#### Explanations

After creating the workers, each worker has an independent seed that is initialized to the curent random seed + the id of the worker. Also, you need to reset the numpy random seed at the beginning of each epoch because all random seed modifications in `__getitem__` are local to each worker.

FYI, `np.random.get_state()[1][0]` allows you to get the seed. For example:
```python
In [1]: np.random.seed(1234)
   ...: np.random.get_state()[1][0]
   ...: 
Out[1]: 1234
``` 

#### Updated Code

```python

import random

# np.random.seed(0)

class Transform(object):
    def __init__(self):
        pass

    def __call__(self, item = None):
        return [np.random.randint(10000, 20000), random.randint(20000,30000)]

class RandomDataset(object):

    def __init__(self):
        pass

    def __getitem__(self, ind):
        item = [ind, np.random.randint(1, 10000), random.randint(10000, 20000), 0]
        tsfm =Transform()(item)
        return np.array(item + tsfm)
    def __len__(self):
        return 20


from torch.utils.data import DataLoader

ds = RandomDataset()
ds = DataLoader(ds, 10, shuffle=False, num_workers=4, worker_init_fn=worker_init_fn)

for epoch in range(2):
    print("epoch {}".format(epoch))
    np.random.seed()
    for batch in ds:
        print(batch)
```
